sections.h: Jesus at the Festival of Shelters (John 7–8)
sections.b: John 7:2–8:59 takes place at the Festival of Shelters, and Jesus' sayings answer its rites. Each morning priests drew water at the pool of Siloam and poured it on the altar, praying for rain (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9); on the last great day Jesus cries, "If anyone is thirsty, he should come to me and drink" (John 7:37). Each night great lamps lit the Court of Women; there Jesus says, "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12, 20). Then he sends a blind man to the waters of Siloam to receive his sight (John 9:7). The festival that remembered God's water and fire in the wilderness becomes, in John, a festival about Jesus.

common: Jesus' words about living water and light were spoken against the background of the festival's water and lamp ceremonies.
uncommon: Some scholars think the healing at Siloam in John 9 is meant as the climax of the festival scenes in John 7–8.

sections.b: John 10:22 is the only mention of Hanukkah in the New Testament and in the Protestant Bible; Catholic and Orthodox Bibles also tell its origin in 1 and 2 Maccabees. In winter, in Solomon's Porch, Jesus is asked whether he is the Messiah, at a festival that celebrated the Maccabees' deliverance and the temple made holy again. He calls himself the one "the Father made holy and sent into the world" (John 10:36), using the language of consecration, and speaks of a shepherd who gives his life, in contrast to thieves and bandits. Christians who keep no Hanukkah of their own meet the festival here.

In these chapters the word covers very different people: the authorities who want Jesus dead (John 7:1, 13), a puzzled crowd (John 7:35), Jews who had believed in him (John 8:31), the questioners of the blind man (John 9:18, 22), and a divided audience (John 10:19). Since every character is Jewish, the word cannot mean the Jewish people as such in these scenes. The harshest line, "You come from your father, the devil" (John 8:44), was spoken in a quarrel with particular opponents; later Christians read it as a verdict on all Jews, from medieval preaching to Luther's 1543 tract and Nazi propaganda, such as Elvira Bauer's 1936 children's book Trust No Fox. The expulsion from the synagogue in John 9:22 is the center of the scholarly debate about the Birkat ha-Minim.

common: John 8:44 was spoken to particular opponents in a dispute among Jews, and is misused when applied to the Jewish people.
uncommon: Some scholars, such as Adele Reinhartz, argue that the Gospel's rhetoric is anti-Jewish in its effect whatever the author intended, so explaining the context is not enough.

sections.h: Light, door, shepherd, and the bare "I am" (John 8–10)
sections.b: John 8–10 has two of the pictured sayings, "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12; 9:5) and the double image of the door and the good shepherd (John 10:7, 9, 11, 14), and three absolute ones (John 8:24, 28, 58). The healed blind man's "I am he" (John 9:9) shows the phrase in its ordinary use and makes Jesus' use stand out. The climax, "before Abraham came to be, I am," draws the response of stoning (John 8:59).

sections.b: Jesus takes up Ezekiel 34, where God condemns shepherds who feed themselves and promises to shepherd his flock himself and to set over them one shepherd, David. He is the shepherd who comes through the door, calls his sheep by name, leads them out, knows them as the Father knows him, and lays down his life for them (John 10:3, 11, 14–15). The hired man runs; the thief kills. The image was spoken to leaders who had just expelled a healed man (John 9:34–41), and it later shaped the Christian idea of the pastor (1 Peter 5:2–4).

The best-known passage not in the earliest manuscripts of the Gospels. It is absent from Papyrus 66 and 75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, appears first in Codex Bezae (400s), wanders to other places (after John 7:36, John 21:25 or Luke 21:38), and has Luke's vocabulary. Yet a story like it was known to Papias and to the Didascalia. NA28 prints it in double brackets, SBLGNT and THGNT give it only in their apparatus, and most Bibles print it in place with a note.

sections.h: Jesus and the death penalty for adultery (John 8:1–11)
sections.b: The law ordered death for both adulterers (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22–24), with witnesses throwing the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7). John 18:31 says that under Rome the Jewish council could not carry out executions, though historians debate how strictly that held. Jesus does not deny the law but asks the one without sin to throw first, and sends the woman away uncondemned with the command to stop sinning. Opponents of the death penalty often cite the story; others answer that it addresses hypocritical accusers and an unlawful trial, not the state's authority to punish.

In John 8:31–58 Jesus argues that descent from Abraham does not make someone his child; doing Abraham's works does (John 8:39–40). He then says Abraham rejoiced to see his day (John 8:56), drawing on Jewish traditions that God showed Abraham the future (Genesis 15; Genesis Rabbah 44:22), and claims, "before Abraham came to be, I am" (John 8:58).

Accused of blasphemy, Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6, "I said, You are gods," and argues that if Scripture calls "gods" those to whom God's word came, he cannot be condemned for calling himself God's Son (John 10:34–36). Readers differ over whether the psalm's "gods" are Israel's judges, Israel at Sinai, or members of God's heavenly council.

Jesus defends a Sabbath healing with an argument from circumcision, which Jewish law already allowed on the Sabbath (John 7:22–23; Mishnah Shabbat 18:3). In John 9 he makes clay, a form of kneading, and heals a man blind from birth on a Sabbath, and the Pharisees divide over whether a Sabbath-breaker can be from God (John 9:14–16).

John says plainly that Jesus' brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5) and shows them urging him to perform in Jerusalem. After Easter they are among the believers (Acts 1:14). The passage is one of those debated between churches over whether the brothers were Mary's sons.

Jesus says that his sheep will never be lost and that no one can snatch them from his hand or the Father's. Reformed and Baptist Christians read this as the security of every true believer; Methodists, Lutherans and Catholics agree that no outside power can take them, but hold that a believer can still turn away.

Jesus has other sheep "not of this fold," whom he must bring so that there will be one flock and one shepherd. Most readers see Gentiles joining believing Israel (compare John 11:52); dispensationalists see the church as a body distinct from national Israel; Latter-day Saints and Jehovah's Witnesses have their own readings.

Jesus says "I and the Father are one" (neuter hen, "one thing"), and is accused of making himself God. He answers that he only said, "I am God's Son" (John 10:36). The fathers used the verse against both Arius ("one") and Sabellius ("are"); Jehovah's Witnesses read it as unity of purpose.

Jesus heals with clay and the waters of Siloam a man blind from birth, something unheard of (John 9:32). He refuses the idea that the blindness was punishment for sin (John 9:3). The healing becomes an enacted parable of sight and blindness.

Asked whether a man's congenital blindness came from his sin or his parents', Jesus says neither. The answer rejects the link between disability and guilt, though readers still debate what it means that the blindness was "so that God's works can be shown."

John 7 records popular expectations: a Messiah of hidden origin (John 7:27), one from David's line and Bethlehem (John 7:42), one who does many signs (John 7:31), and a separate end-time Prophet (John 7:40–41).
John explains Jesus' promise of living water as the Spirit, who "had not yet come" because Jesus had not yet been glorified. The Spirit is given after the cross and resurrection (John 20:22).

sections.h: The devil as killer and liar (John 8:44)
sections.b: Jesus calls the devil a killer of people from the start and the father of falsehood, linking the lie in Eden (Genesis 3:4) and Cain's murder (Genesis 4:8). The verse is often cited for the devil's character; its use against Jews is a misreading.
